title: Short Stuff: Squarer Than Wombat Poop
summary: Short Stuff episode on wombat poop. Josh and Chuck explain that wombats are the only known animal that produces cube-shaped feces, starting with the phrase "square as a wombat" and a description of wombats as stout, powerful diggers related to koalas, weighing up to about 77 pounds (35 kg). They describe the early assumption that the square shape came from a square-shaped rectum, and how a researcher checked and found a normal round anus. They cover the Australian study at the University of Tasmania, where a wombat hit by a car was dissected and researcher Dr. Scott Carver found grooves and differing elasticity in the intestines, and the later Georgia Tech study by biomechanics researcher David Hu's team, published in the journal Soft Matter, which found the last portion of the intestine has stiff and elastic regions that move differently, shaping the poop. They note the wombat's intestine is very long relative to its body, digestion is slow, and the poop is very dry. The hosts speculate that square poop helps wombats mark territory on rocks and logs without rolling away, and mention that dry square poop can indicate a healthy wombat in captivity. The episode ends with a sign-off.
topics: David Hu Georgia Tech wombat study

segments.title: Introduction and the 'square as a wombat' saying
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the short about wombats and square poop, which grew out of a previous episode's discussion of digestion. They joke about the saying 'square as a wombat' and say they had not heard it before.

segments.title: Wombat description and cube-shaped poop
segments.summary: Wombats are described as stout, short-legged, powerful diggers with long claws, related to koalas, weighing up to about 77 pounds (35 kg). They are territorial and mark trails with scent and cube-shaped droppings, which are said to be produced about a hundred times a day.

segments.title: Early assumptions about the square shape
segments.summary: Hosts describe how early researchers assumed a square-shaped rectum, but examination found a normal round anus, with a researcher checking by hand.

segments.title: Australian and Georgia Tech dissection studies
segments.summary: A wombat hit by a car at the University of Tasmania was dissected by Dr. Scott Carver, who found grooves and differing elasticity in the intestines. Later, David Hu's biomechanics team at Georgia Tech studied wombat intestines and published findings on why the poop is square.
topics: David Hu Georgia Tech wombat study

segments.title: How the intestines shape the poop
segments.summary: The Georgia Tech team found stiff and elastic regions in the final part of the wombat intestine that contract differently, producing the square shape. The intestine is about ten times the animal's body length, and digestion takes about four times longer than in humans, leaving very dry feces.

segments.title: Why square poop evolved and practical uses
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the theory that square droppings stay put on rocks and logs for territorial marking. Hu's team is described as publishing in Soft Matter and receiving an Ig Nobel Prize. The hosts note the findings could inspire biomechanical design and that dry square poop may indicate a healthy wombat in captivity.

segments.title: Closing banter and sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close with jokes about the topic and a pollen-related laugh, followed by the standard sign-off and iHeartRadio credit.
